parts.move: state the definition of electric current and the quantity it measures
parts.prompt: Define electric current in terms of charge, and state its SI unit.
scheme: Current is the rate of flow of electric charge: I = ΔQ/Δt
The unit is the ampere (A), where 1 A = 1 C s⁻¹
parts.answer: Electric current is the rate of flow of charge, I = ΔQ/Δt. One ampere is one coulomb of charge passing a point each second.

parts.move: state Ohm's law with its condition of validity
parts.prompt: State Ohm's law and state the condition under which it holds for a conductor.
scheme: The current through a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across it: V = IR
It holds when resistance is constant — temperature and other physical conditions unchanged
parts.answer: Ohm's law: V = IR — the potential difference is proportional to the current. It holds only while the resistance stays constant, typically at fixed temperature; a filament lamp's rising temperature breaks the proportionality.

parts.move: explain why series components share one current from charge conservation
parts.prompt: Explain why the current is the same at every point in a series circuit, even through components of different resistance.
scheme: Charge is conserved — it cannot pile up or vanish inside a component
Whatever charge flows in must flow out at the same rate in steady state
So the same current passes through every element in the single loop
parts.answer: Charge is conserved: in steady state it cannot accumulate at any point. The rate of flow entering each component must equal the rate leaving it, so one common current threads the whole series loop, whatever the resistances.

parts.move: explain why parallel branches lower total resistance
parts.prompt: Adding a resistor in parallel reduces the total resistance of a circuit. Explain this in terms of the routes the charge can take.
scheme: Each parallel branch gives charge an additional independent route
The supply can push more total current for the same voltage
R_total = V/I_total falls because I_total is the sum of branch currents
parts.answer: A parallel branch is one more route the charge can take. At the same applied voltage each route carries its own current, and the supply delivers the sum — more current for the same V means a smaller effective resistance. More paths, more flow.

parts.move: reject the claim that current gets consumed by components
parts.prompt: A student measures 0.5 A entering a lamp and expects less current to leave it, saying the lamp 'uses up current'. Explain the error, and state what the lamp actually uses up.
scheme: Charge is conserved: current in equals current out (0.5 A both sides)
The lamp converts electrical energy to heat and light, not charge
What decreases across the lamp is electrical potential — energy per coulomb
parts.answer: The current leaving is the same 0.5 A that enters — charge is conserved and the lamp stores none of it. What the lamp consumes is energy: each coulomb passes through at a lower potential, dropping V volts, and that energy per unit charge becomes heat and light.

parts.move: reject treating terminal voltage as fixed equal to emf under load
parts.prompt: A student says a 12 V battery always supplies 12 V across its terminals, whatever the load. Explain why heavy loads read lower, using internal resistance.
scheme: A real battery has internal resistance r in series with its emf
Under current I, the terminal voltage is V = ε − Ir
Heavy loads draw large I, dropping more volts inside the battery — the terminal voltage sags
parts.answer: A real battery behaves as an ideal emf ε in series with an internal resistance r. The terminals deliver V = ε − Ir; a heavy load draws a large current, and the volts lost inside (Ir) grow, so the terminal reading falls below 12 V — the starter motor dims the headlights.

parts.move: reduce a series-parallel network and solve for current and voltages
parts.prompt: A 12 V battery of negligible internal resistance feeds a 4.0 Ω resistor in series with a parallel pair of 6.0 Ω and 3.0 Ω. Calculate the total current drawn and the potential difference across the parallel pair.
scheme: V_parallel = 2.0 A × 2.0 Ω = 4.0 V (leaving 8.0 V across the series resistor)
parts.answer: The parallel pair reduces to (6×3)/(6+3) = 2.0 Ω, so the loop totals 6.0 Ω and draws I = 12/6 = 2.0 A. The parallel section then sees V = 2.0×2.0 = 4.0 V, with the remaining 8.0 V across the series resistor.

parts.move: transfer circuit relations to household appliance ratings
parts.prompt: A kettle is rated 2.4 kW at 240 V and a toaster 960 W at 240 V, both plugged into the same wall socket circuit. Calculate the current each draws and the combined current when both run together, explaining why this matters for a 13 A fuse.
scheme: Kettle: I = P/V = 2400/240 = 10 A
Toaster: I = 960/240 = 4.0 A
Together: 14 A (loads in parallel, currents add)
14 A exceeds a 13 A fuse — running both on one circuit blows it
parts.answer: The kettle draws 2400/240 = 10 A and the toaster 960/240 = 4.0 A; in parallel their currents add to 14 A. That exceeds the 13 A protection of the fused spur, so running both together from one socket blows the fuse — the safety margin is exactly this addition.

parts.move: transfer potential-divider reasoning to a thermistor sensing circuit
parts.prompt: A thermistor has resistance 10 kΩ at 20 °C falling to 2.0 kΩ at 60 °C. It is placed in a potential divider with a fixed 5.0 kΩ resistor across a 6.0 V supply, with the output taken across the thermistor. Calculate the output voltage at 20 °C and at 60 °C.
scheme: The divider converts the thermistor's resistance change into a voltage change
2.3 V swing across the 40 °C range — a usable sensor signal
parts.answer: At 20 °C the divider gives V_out = 6×10/15 = 4.0 V; at 60 °C, V_out = 6×2/7 = 1.7 V. The thermistor's resistance fall with temperature is translated into a 2.3 V drop — precisely how electronic thermometers turn temperature into a readable voltage.

parts.move: combine power relations with cable resistance to find transmission efficiency
parts.prompt: A generator supplies 2.0 kW at 250 V through a cable of total resistance 3.0 Ω to a load designed for that voltage. Calculate the cable power loss, the power received, and the transmission efficiency, then state one way to improve it.
scheme: Current I = P/V = 2000/250 = 8.0 A
Cable loss P = I²R = 64 × 3.0 = 192 W
Received power = 2000 − 192 = 1808 W; efficiency = 1808/2000 = 90.4%
Transmit at higher voltage: I = P/V falls, and loss ∝ I² falls as the square
parts.answer: The 2.0 kW at 250 V implies I = 8.0 A, losing I²R = 192 W in the cable, so 1808 W arrives — 90% efficiency. Raising the transmission voltage cuts the current in proportion, and the quadratic loss with it: that is the entire logic of high-voltage grids.

parts.move: combine I-V interpretation with power accounting for a non-ohmic device
parts.prompt: A filament lamp's I-V graph curves so that at 2.0 V it passes 0.20 A and at 6.0 V it passes 0.30 A. Compare its resistance at the two points, and calculate the power dissipated at each.
scheme: The resistance has doubled: the hotter filament scatters electrons more
parts.answer: At 2.0 V the lamp's resistance is 10 Ω; at 6.0 V it is 20 Ω — the hotter filament lattice impedes the current more, hence the flattening curve. Dissipated power rises from 0.40 W to 1.8 W, and it is this self-heating that makes the device non-ohmic in the first place.
